bibl.title: Dos and don’ts in response priming research

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: method
span.quote: Our intention here is to give an introduction to methodological issues involved in response priming.

span.label: response priming
span.quote: Response priming refers to a situation in which a participant is reacting to a target stimulus as quickly and accurately as possible.

span.label: review
span.quote: We discuss the major opportunities of the paradigm and give specific recommendations (e.g., tracing the time-course of priming in parametric experiments).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: The prime activates the response mapped to it, and the longer the delay before the target arrives the longer the prime alone can drive that response, which is why priming grows with SOA
span.quote: Such data suggest that the prime activates a response assigned to it, and has more time to drive the response on its own the more time elapses between prime and target.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Backward masking works by disrupting recurrent processing, which is what awareness depends on, while priming rides the earlier feedforward sweep and is therefore left intact
span.quote: Because backward masking works through disruption of recurrent processing (cf. DiLollo, Enns, & Rensink, 2000 ; Fahrenfort, Scholte, & Lamme, 2007 ; Lamme, Zipser, & Spekreijse, 2002 ), it does not affect response priming effects resulting from feedforward activation.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Participants guess prime identity from perceived flicker, and because flicker itself grows with prime-target SOA, this strategy produces the SOA-dependent reversal of bias in prime identification
span.quote: However, the amount of flicker is in fact driven primarily by the prime-target SOA, with more flicker at longer SOAs.

span.label: The recommendations are deliberately not to be followed dogmatically; deliberately violating them can be theoretically informative.
span.quote: It shouldn’t be observed too dogmatically: Even though it is wise to avoid certain mistakes and artifacts, in some situations it will be of theoretical interest to systematically go against those recommendations.

span.label: The dos-and-don'ts list is explicitly incomplete.
span.quote: In the end, everything will be condensed into a non-comprehensive list of “Dos and Don’ts” which we hope will be helpful to newcomers to the field.

span.label: The recommendation to separate direct and indirect tasks into blocks rests on evidence that is missing for direct measures.
span.quote: Regarding direct measures, however, syste-matic comparisons between the single-task and dual-task approaches are still missing.

span.label: Guidance on three-stimulus (prime-mask-target) designs is limited by unresolved knowledge about motor activation in that situation.
span.quote: However, the time-course of motor activation in the three-stimulus situation is not well understood, and intervening masks seem to be able to interact with primes and targets on a motor level.

span.label: the argument against discarding subjects who fail an awareness check is made by analogy with a clinical trial: excluding those subjects is like removing from the analysis the patients the drug killed
span.quote: Actually, the practice is analogous to eliminating all the patients from a clinical trial that have died from the drug under investigation.

span.label: zero sensitivity criterion
span.quote: double-dissociations overcome the problem of the traditional zero sensitivity criterion , which demands that priming effects must be demonstrated under conditions where sensitivity to the prime is exactly zero (i.e., when the prime is “invisible”). This criterion is seemingly strict but implies strong measurement assumptions which are not required for double dissociations

span.label: double dissociation
span.quote: courses of priming and prime visibility can form a double dissociation where both variables develop in opposite directions ( Schmidt & Vorberg, 2006 ; also see Merikle & Joordens, 1997a , 1997b ). For instance, if response priming is combined with type-B masking, there will be a range of prime-mask SOAs that lead to decreasing visibility of the prime yet increasing priming effects. Under very mild measurement assumptions, double dissociations imply that priming and awareness cannot both be driven by a single source of conscious information, thus refuting the idea that priming effects may simply measure residual conscious information about the prime not detected by the prime identification task

span.label: prime visibility
span.quote: courses of priming and prime visibility can form a double dissociation where both variables develop in opposite directions ( Schmidt & Vorberg, 2006 ; also see Merikle & Joordens, 1997a , 1997b ). For instance, if response priming is combined with type-B masking, there will be a range of prime-mask SOAs that lead to decreasing visibility of the prime yet increasing priming effects. Under very mild measurement assumptions, double dissociations imply that priming and awareness cannot both be driven by a single source of conscious information, thus refuting the idea that priming effects may simply measure residual conscious information about the prime not detected by the prime identification task

span.label: response priming
span.quote: This makes response priming well suited for parametric variation of the independent va-riables, and in fact the paradigm unfolds its true power only in parametric experiments

span.label: visual awareness
span.quote: A fascinating feature of response priming is its independence of visual awareness. The relationship between both can be investigated by combining response priming with methods of visual masking: If primes are rendered invisible by presentation of another stimulus in close temporal proximity (the mask ), priming effects typically remain unchanged. By using metacontrast masking ( Breitmeyer & Ömen, 2006 ), a form of masking that we will describe later, response time effects and visual awareness can even be double-dissociated: When the visibility of the primes decreases, priming effects can still increase ( Albrecht, Klapötke, & Mattler, 2010 ; Mattler, 2003b ; Vorberg et al., 2003 ). Thus, for a short time and under suitable experimental conditions, visually masked stimuli can influence motor responses just as effectively as clearly perceivable stimuli. This independence of visual awareness and motor activation makes response priming a particularly useful tool in studying early visual processing

span.label: evidence as a SHAPE rather than a LEVEL - the double dissociation replaces `awareness must be zero` with `awareness and priming must move in opposite directions across SOAs`. If a range of prime-mask SOAs shows visibility DECREASING while priming INCREASES, then the two cannot both be driven by one source of conscious information. The criterion needs a time-course, not a threshold - the sixth time this sitting that a time course is the load-bearing variable
span.quote: courses of priming and prime visibility can form a double dissociation where both variables develop in opposite directions ( Schmidt & Vorberg, 2006 ; also see Merikle & Joordens, 1997a , 1997b ). For instance, if response priming is combined with type-B masking, there will be a range of prime-mask SOAs that lead to decreasing visibility of the prime yet increasing priming effects. Under very mild measurement assumptions, double dissociations imply that priming and awareness cannot both be driven by a single source of conscious information, thus refuting the idea that priming effects may simply measure residual conscious information about the prime not detected by the prime identification task

span.label: A DESIGN FLAW THAT MANUFACTURES THE CORRELATION IT IS USED TO SHOW: varying the prime's duration while leaving the prime-target ISI constant confounds prime duration with SOA and `creates a SPURIOUS CORRELATION between priming and prime visibility by two mechanisms` - a stronger prime gives stronger priming, and a longer SOA gives stronger priming. The fix is to leave the prime intact and control visibility by varying the MASK. A confound that produces apparent evidence for a link between priming and awareness out of the timing alone
span.quote: Unless variation of the prime is of theoretical interest, it is therefore crucial to leave the prime intact and control its visibility by variation of mask attributes only (e.g., its stimulus contrast). With higher mask energy, visual awareness for the prime should diminish ( Breitmeyer & Ömen, 2006 ). This way, visual awareness can be varied indepen-dently of prime-mask SOA

span.label: the paradigm's power located in PARAMETRIC VARIATION rather than in a single contrast: response priming effects are `numerically large ... and pretty stable across individuals`, so the recommendation is to trace them across a range of SOAs. `The paradigm unfolds its true power ONLY IN PARAMETRIC EXPERIMENTS` - a methods paper telling its field that one comparison is not the way to use its own tool
span.quote: This makes response priming well suited for parametric variation of the independent va-riables, and in fact the paradigm unfolds its true power only in parametric experiments

span.label: THE ZERO SENSITIVITY CRITERION, AND WHY IT IS UNMEETABLE - not `too strict`, but resting on an instrument that does not exist: it `requires an exhaustive measure of visual awareness which is GUARANTEED TO NEVER MISS A CHANGE in visual awareness, however tiny`. A standard whose satisfaction cannot be established, which is a different failing from a standard that is hard to reach. Second record in a row retiring a criterion on this ground (see Kiefer2012, Q-755)
span.quote: double-dissociations overcome the problem of the traditional zero sensitivity criterion , which demands that priming effects must be demonstrated under conditions where sensitivity to the prime is exactly zero (i.e., when the prime is “invisible”). This criterion is seemingly strict but implies strong measurement assumptions which are not required for double dissociations

span.label: builds-on → existing theories of response priming: direct parameter specification (Neumann, 1990), the action trigger account (Kunde, Kiesel, & Hoffmann, 2003) and rapid-chase theory (Schmidt et al., 2006)
span.quote: In our opinion, the basic mechanisms of response priming are now reasonably well understood and have led to detailed and successful theories (e.g., the principle of direct parameter specification by Neumann, 1990 ; the action trigger account by Kunde, Kiesel, & Hoffmann, 2003 ; and the rapid-chase theory by Schmidt et al., 2006 ).

span.label: builds-on → the direct/indirect task-matching recommendations of Schmidt and Vorberg (2006)
span.quote: Following the recommendations by Schmidt and Vorberg ( 2006 ) , we strongly recommend that direct and indirect tasks be matched with respect to (a) the stimuli, (b) the features to be judged, and (c) the assignment of those features to motor responses.

span.label: contradicts → the zero sensitivity criterion for masked priming research
span.quote: In fact, the common preconception of many researchers (and many reviewers) that masked priming experiments require zero sensitivity for the prime is a fallacy, because double dissociations are invariably more informative, more powerful, and less assumption-ridden.

span.label: builds-on → the feedforward sweep account of Lamme and Roelfsema (2000)
span.quote: Applied to response priming, this theory can explain why response priming effects remain intact under visual backward masking of the prime: Because backward masking works through disruption of recurrent processing (cf. DiLollo, Enns, & Rensink, 2000 ; Fahrenfort, Scholte, & Lamme, 2007 ; Lamme, Zipser, & Spekreijse, 2002 ), it does not affect response priming effects resulting from feedforward activation.

span.label: double dissociation —operationalised-as→ prime visibility
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9 — What the dissociation is made OF: two time-courses, priming and prime visibility, measured over the same SOA range and required to diverge. The measure is the pair, not either curve alone.
span.quote: courses of priming and prime visibility can form a double dissociation where both variables develop in opposite directions ( Schmidt & Vorberg, 2006 ; also see Merikle & Joordens, 1997a , 1997b ). For instance, if response priming is combined with type-B masking, there will be a range of prime-mask SOAs that lead to decreasing visibility of the prime yet increasing priming effects. Under very mild measurement assumptions, double dissociations imply that priming and awareness cannot both be driven by a single source of conscious information, thus refuting the idea that priming effects may simply measure residual conscious information about the prime not detected by the prime identification task

span.label: response priming —distinct-from→ visual awareness
span.note: differs in: WHETHER ONE CAN BE READ OFF THE OTHER - masked stimuli `can influence motor responses just as effectively as clearly perceivable stimuli`, so the motor effect does not track what was seen. That independence is what the paper calls the paradigm's useful feature rather than a nuisance · strength of the relation: 0.9 — Re-grounded off the zero-sensitivity passage, which never names `response priming`. This sentence pair names both endpoints, is free of brackets, and states the separation as the paradigm's defining property. Weighted 0.9: the paper is a methods review reporting an established feature, not an experiment establishing it here.
span.quote: A fascinating feature of response priming is its independence of visual awareness. The relationship between both can be investigated by combining response priming with methods of visual masking: If primes are rendered invisible by presentation of another stimulus in close temporal proximity (the mask ), priming effects typically remain unchanged. By using metacontrast masking ( Breitmeyer & Ömen, 2006 ), a form of masking that we will describe later, response time effects and visual awareness can even be double-dissociated: When the visibility of the primes decreases, priming effects can still increase ( Albrecht, Klapötke, & Mattler, 2010 ; Mattler, 2003b ; Vorberg et al., 2003 ). Thus, for a short time and under suitable experimental conditions, visually masked stimuli can influence motor responses just as effectively as clearly perceivable stimuli. This independence of visual awareness and motor activation makes response priming a particularly useful tool in studying early visual processing

span.label: Response priming effects are unusually large for reaction-time research, accounting for a quarter or more of the total response time, which is why small samples suffice and extensive parametric variation is practical.
span.quote: Response priming effects are among the numerically largest effects in response time research; they can account for 25% or more of the overall response time.

span.label: Priming effects grow the longer the interval between prime and target onset, because the prime has more time to drive the response before the target takes over motor control.
span.quote: The longer the prime signal can control the motor response before the target signal does, the stronger the prime’s influence on the output variables

span.label: Priming and visual awareness can move in opposite directions: priming effects can keep increasing while the prime becomes less visible, which is a double dissociation.
span.quote: When the visibility of the primes decreases, priming effects can still increase

span.label: Reducing prime visibility by weakening the prime itself is a design flaw, because weakening the prime also weakens priming, so the direct and indirect measures are necessarily confounded and appear correlated.
span.quote: in any design which modifies visibility by varying the prime, the indirect measures (e.g., priming task) and direct measures (e.g., prime identification task) are always confounded.

span.label: Computing the sensitivity measure d' separately for consistent and inconsistent trials is invalid because it mixes sensitivity with response bias; d' should instead be computed separately for different target types.
span.quote: Calculating the sensitivity measure d’ separately for consistent and inconsistent trials confounds sensitivity and bias.

span.label: Excluding participants whose prime identification is above chance is a sampling fallacy, since dropping observations does not alter the population the sample came from.
span.quote: Discarding some observations from the sample does not change the underlying population on which the sample is based.

span.label: Prime identification performance carries an SOA-dependent bias: participants lean toward the target's direction at short SOAs and away from it at long SOAs.
span.quote: As a result, responses reveal a strong bias in target direction at short SOAs, but a bias against target direction at long SOAs

span.label: The authors recommend varying prime-target SOA in at least three steps across the whole range of interest, roughly 0 to 100 ms, rather than testing a single SOA.
span.quote: Our recommendation is that in every response priming experiment, the SOA should be varied in at least three steps, covering the whole time range of interest (e.g., from 0 to 100 ms).

span.label: About 60 trials per condition per participant is enough to yield small standard errors and to allow single-participant data patterns to be evaluated.
span.quote: To produce reliable data patterns with relatively small standard errors, around 60 trials per condition and participant has turned out to be a reasonable number

span.label: Direct and indirect tasks must be matched on the stimuli used, the features judged, and how those features map onto motor responses, otherwise the direct task loses validity as a measure of awareness of the prime.
span.quote: we strongly recommend that direct and indirect tasks be matched with respect to (a) the stimuli, (b) the features to be judged, and (c) the assignment of those features to motor responses

span.label: Error rates in inconsistent trials index response activation by the prime just as response times do, so they deserve equally careful analysis.
span.quote: priming effects in error rates are of similar importance as the response time effects and should be analyzed just as carefully

span.label: The earliest phase of response activation is controlled by prime information alone and is unaffected by the target, so prime and target take control of the response in strict sequence.
span.quote: These studies show that the earliest processes of response activation are determined exclusively by prime information but are independent of all target information

span.label: response priming
span.quote: Response priming refers to a situation in which a participant is reacting to a target stimulus as quickly and accurately as possible.

span.label: priming effect
span.quote: leading to priming effects usually defined as the response time difference between consistent and inconsistent trials

span.label: priming function
span.quote: the resulting priming function (the priming effect as a function of prime-target SOA) follows a prototypical pattern where priming effects increase approximately linearly with SOA

span.label: interstimulus interval (ISI)
span.quote: tightly linked to the interstimulus interval , ISI, which is defined as the time between the offset of the prime and the onset of the target

span.label: feedforward sweep
span.quote: propose that a novel stimulus elicits a wave of neuronal feedforward activation ( feedforward sweep ) rushing through the visuomotor system

span.label: metacontrast masking
span.quote: A type of masking often used in response priming studies is metacontrast , a form of backward masking in which the inner contours of a hollow masking stimulus are bordering the outer contours of the previously presented prime

span.label: type-A masking
span.quote: In type-A masking , prime visibility is lowest at short prime-mask SOAs and increases with increasing SOA

span.label: type-B masking
span.quote: type-B masking occurs under specific circumstances in metacontrast masking. Here, visibility is lowest at medium SOAs (often, around 50 ms) and higher at shorter or longer SOAs

span.label: prime identification task
span.quote: The amount of masking (or prime visibility) is measured by administration of a prime identification task , in which the participant is asked to detect, identify, or categorize the prime, or to indicate its subjective visibility.

span.label: zero sensitivity criterion
span.quote: double-dissociations overcome the problem of the traditional zero sensitivity criterion , which demands that priming effects must be demonstrated under conditions where sensitivity to the prime is exactly zero

span.label: prime-target stimulus onset asynchrony (SOA)
span.quote: Our recommendation is that in every response priming experiment, the SOA should be varied in at least three steps, covering the whole time range of interest (e.g., from 0 to 100 ms).

span.label: priming effect in response times and error rates
span.term: priming effect in response times and error rates
span.quote: priming effects in error rates are of similar importance as the response time effects and should be analyzed just as carefully

span.label: prime visibility
span.quote: The amount of masking (or prime visibility) is measured by administration of a prime identification task , in which the participant is asked to detect, identify, or categorize the prime, or to indicate its subjective visibility.

span.label: prime presentation duration
span.quote: Primes are always presented for 12 ms, only the time interval between prime and target presentation is systematically varied.

span.label: prime stimulus energy (left unmodified while mask attributes are varied)
span.term: prime stimulus energy (left unmodified while mask attributes are varied)
span.quote: it is therefore crucial to leave the prime intact and control its visibility by variation of mask attributes only (e.g., its stimulus contrast)

span.label: 25% — Share of overall response time that response priming effects can account for
span.quote: Response priming effects are among the numerically largest effects in response time research; they can account for 25% or more of the overall response time.

span.label: 60 — Recommended number of trials per condition per participant
span.quote: To produce reliable data patterns with relatively small standard errors, around 60 trials per condition and participant has turned out to be a reasonable number

span.label: three steps — Minimum number of SOA levels the authors recommend sampling, over a 0-100 ms range
span.quote: Our recommendation is that in every response priming experiment, the SOA should be varied in at least three steps, covering the whole time range of interest (e.g., from 0 to 100 ms).

span.label: 100 ms — SOA below which the prototypical, approximately linear priming function is obtained
span.quote: If prime and target presentations follow each other at stimulus-onset asynchronies (SOAs) shorter than about 100 ms

span.label: 12 ms — Fixed prime presentation duration in the typical experiment illustrated
span.quote: Primes are always presented for 12 ms, only the time interval between prime and target presentation is systematically varied.

span.label: 50 ms — Approximate prime-mask SOA at which prime visibility is lowest under type-B masking
span.quote: type-B masking occurs under specific circumstances in metacontrast masking. Here, visibility is lowest at medium SOAs (often, around 50 ms) and higher at shorter or longer SOAs
